title: “The Body of Mary: A Play in Three Acts (Of God)” runs in NYC through...
transcript: Three unwanted pregnancies tied to Catholicism in different ways, from the mother of Jesus to a group of aging nuns to a teenage Dairy Queen worker. This new play, The Body of Mary, tells three stories that seem to stand alone, but all muse on the same theme and all focus on a character named Mary. Playwright and director Katie Cappiello first imagines: what if Mary of Nazareth wasn't so pleased to learn that she had been impregnated by God without her consent? Then we move into the 21st century, where she imagines a deliberately outlandish scheme concocted by a corrupt priest in a near future where abortion has been completely outlawed. Then we end with a teenager discovering a baby in a dumpster and working through the logistical question of what to do with her, but also the emotional exercise of empathizing with someone desperate enough to leave her there. It feels like Cappiello is fueled by deep frustration and a nagging personal drive to untangle the knotted links between Catholicism and pregnancy. And, you know, I should mention, as someone with no personal ties to Catholicism, I don't necessarily have the cultural perspective to assess how spot-on her insights are here. But for what it's worth, I did find it very thought provoking and moving, especially in the more serious third act. The first two acts have a surprising amount of comedy in them, using very heightened satire to skewer the ironies and hypocrisies in the Catholic Church. Because of that I understood why Cappiello wanted to direct it herself. There's such a specific tone that precariously balances the humor with the more serious commentary. And I think she successfully cast and directed it to capture the energy that she was going for. Broadly speaking, I would also say that it was just very well acted. So I was surprised then to find that I was feeling a bit more cold toward it the next day. It didn't feel quite as successful in retrospect as it did in the moment, and I've been trying to pinpoint why that is. I do wonder if it has to do with the humor, because in a way, the structure and the concept already were successfully making her point. And so spinning these kind of parable-esque stories into heightened satire was maybe just not necessary. So even though I found it funny in the moment, it was, maybe, undercutting the drama and kind of dampening the effect of it in a way they didn't really notice until I was sitting with it for a couple days.
